title: Victorian Names
seoTitle: Victorian Names: 105 Popular Girl and Boy Names
description: Ada, Florence, Edith, Albert, Arthur, Percy: 105 names that were really common in Victorian England, all in the official 1904 top 100, with meanings.
intro:
These are names Victorian families actually used. There are no official rankings for Queen Victoria's reign (1837–1901), so we used the closest reliable evidence: the Office for National Statistics top 100 for babies born in 1904, the earliest official list, plus Douglas Galbi's study of name frequencies in England and Wales through the 1800s. Every name here was in the ONS top 100 for girls or boys born in 1904.

Meanings come from Behind the Name. Many Victorian favourites were revivals of medieval or Old English names, and a few, like Ethel and Daisy, were brand new in the 1800s.

names.name: Mary
names.meaning: possibly from an Egyptian word for "beloved" or "love"
names.note: the top girls' name for most of the century

names.name: Florence
names.note: also given after the Italian city, as with Florence Nightingale, who was born there

names.name: Edith
names.meaning: from Old English Eadgyth, prosperity + war

names.name: Annie
names.meaning: pet form of Anne, from Hebrew Hannah, "favour, grace"

names.name: Winifred
names.meaning: possibly from the Welsh name Gwenfrewi
names.note: the origin is not certain

names.name: Ethel
names.meaning: short form of Old English names beginning æthel, "noble"
names.note: first used on its own in the 1800s

names.name: Hilda
names.note: revived in the 1800s

names.name: Lilian
names.meaning: probably a pet form of Elizabeth; later linked to the lily

names.name: Violet
names.note: came into general English use in the 1800s

names.name: Lily
names.meaning: from the flower name, from Latin lilium

names.name: Nellie
names.meaning: pet form of Nell, itself from Eleanor, Ellen or Helen

names.name: Emily
names.meaning: feminine of the Roman family name Aemilius

names.name: Mabel
names.note: revived in the 1800s

names.name: Ada
names.meaning: short form of Germanic names beginning adal, "noble"
names.note: borne by Ada Lovelace (1815–1852)

names.name: Beatrice
names.meaning: probably from Latin Viatrix, "traveller", later linked to beatus, "blessed"

names.name: May
names.meaning: from the month, or a pet form of Mary or Margaret

names.name: Rose
names.meaning: from a Germanic name meaning "famous kind", soon linked to the flower

names.name: Olive
names.meaning: from the name of the tree

names.name: Grace
names.note: first used by the Puritans; very popular at the end of the 1800s

names.name: Eva
names.meaning: Latin form of Eve, from Hebrew for "to breathe" or "to live"

names.name: Amy
names.note: revived in the 1800s

names.name: Daisy
names.meaning: from the flower, Old English dæges eage, "day's eye"
names.note: first used as a name in the 1800s

names.name: Maud
names.meaning: medieval form of Matilda, "strength in battle"
names.note: revived after Tennyson's poem Maud (1855)

names.name: Lucy
names.meaning: from Latin Lucia, feminine of Lucius

names.name: Emma
names.meaning: from a Germanic element meaning "whole, great"

names.name: Eleanor
names.meaning: from the Occitan name Alienòr; origin uncertain

names.name: Louisa
names.origin: Latin form of a Germanic name

names.name: Dora
names.meaning: short form of Dorothy or Theodora, "gift of God"

names.name: Ida
names.meaning: from a Germanic element possibly meaning "work"

names.name: Isabella
names.meaning: Latin form of Isabel, from Elizabeth

names.name: Harriet
names.meaning: English form of Henriette, from Henry, "home ruler"

names.name: Amelia
names.note: often confused with Emilia

names.name: Lydia
names.meaning: from Lydia, a region of Asia Minor

names.name: William
names.note: the top boys' name from the 1840s to 1900

names.name: John
names.note: the top boys' name at the start of the century

names.name: Arthur
names.meaning: unknown; possibly from Celtic words for "bear", or from the Roman name Artorius

names.name: Albert
names.note: made popular again by Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's husband

names.name: Ernest
names.note: brought to Britain with the House of Hanover

names.name: Alfred
names.note: revived in the 1700s

names.name: Frank
names.meaning: a Frank, a member of the Germanic tribe

names.name: Stanley
names.meaning: stone clearing, from a surname and place name

names.name: Sidney
names.meaning: from the surname of the Sidney family
names.note: first used in honour of the politician Algernon Sidney

names.name: Percy
names.meaning: from the surname of the Percy family, from a Norman place name

names.name: Wilfred
names.note: revived in the 1800s

names.name: Samuel
names.meaning: name of God, or God has heard

names.name: Cecil
names.meaning: from the Roman family name Caecilius
names.note: common from the 1800s, after the Cecil family, whose surname came from the Welsh name Seisyll

names.name: Horace
names.meaning: from Horatius, the Roman poet's family name

names.name: Edwin
names.note: revived in the 1800s

names.name: Victor
names.note: came into general English use in the 1800s

names.name: Ralph
names.meaning: from Old Norse Ráðúlfr, counsel + wolf

names.name: Bertie
names.meaning: pet form of Albert, Herbert and other -bert names

names.name: Percival
names.meaning: invented by the poet Chrétien de Troyes; perhaps "pierce the valley"

names.name: Clarence
names.meaning: from the royal title Duke of Clarence, from Clare in Suffolk

names.name: Oliver
names.meaning: possibly from Latin oliva, "olive tree"; a Germanic origin has also been suggested

sections.heading: How we know these names were popular
sections.content:
Civil registration of births in England and Wales began in 1837, the year Victoria came to the throne, but the government did not publish lists of popular names until much later. The earliest official figures are the ONS top 100 for 1904, three years after Victoria died. Children named in 1904 were given names their parents' generation knew, so the list is a fair picture of late Victorian taste, though not of the 1840s.

For the earlier part of the century, Douglas Galbi's analysis of name samples shows how concentrated naming was: in 1800 Mary and John were each given to more than one child in five, and William overtook John as the top boys' name around 1840. By 1900 the ten commonest names covered far fewer children than in 1800, as parents spread across a wider range.

sections.heading: Revivals, royals and flowers
sections.content:
Three fashions shaped Victorian naming. The first was the revival of Old English and medieval names, encouraged by novels and an interest in the national past: Alice, Edith, Hilda, Maud and Mabel all came back in the 1800s, and Arthur, used in England since the Middle Ages, had a surge in popularity. The second was royalty: Albert had long been rare in England until Prince Albert, Victoria's husband, made it popular again.

The third was flower and plant names. Violet, Ivy, Lily, Daisy and Rose were all in the 1904 top 50 for girls. Violet came into general English use and Daisy was first used as a name in the 1800s, and Rose, an old name, was revived with the flower in mind.

sections.heading: Using a Victorian name today
sections.content:
Many of these names have come back. Florence, Ada, Alice, Arthur, Albert and Alfred are all in recent England and Wales rankings, while Gertrude, Mildred, Horace and Cyril are still rare. The ranking shown with each name is its recent position, so you can see which ones are popular again and which would still stand out.

For a period story, remember that the top few names were far more common then than any name is now: around 1900 about one boy in eleven was still called William, so a schoolroom of Williams, Johns and Georges is no exaggeration.

faqs.question: What were common Victorian names?
faqs.answer: For girls: Mary, Florence, Edith, Annie, Alice, Elizabeth, Elsie, Ethel and Ada. For boys: William, John, George, Thomas, Arthur, James, Charles, Frederick and Albert. All were in the top 25 for babies born in England and Wales in 1904, the earliest official list.

faqs.question: What are some unique Victorian girl names?
faqs.answer: Names that were common then but rare now include Gertrude, Millicent, Blanche, Bertha, Minnie and Edna. All were in the 1904 top 100 for girls in England and Wales.

faqs.question: Why were so many Victorian children called William and Mary?
faqs.answer: Naming was much more concentrated in the 1800s. In 1850 about 15 per cent of boys were called William and 18 per cent of girls Mary, compared with about 4 per cent for the top names in the 1990s.
